Why is this so? Because ultimate quiescence is fundamentally pure like space and cannot be grasped; all realms are likewise! There is no interior, no exterior, and no middle. Realms are not realms;

they are entirely without attachment and entirely without arising. The wise do not give rise to anything, nor do they obtain anything. They neither abide nor do not abide; they are neither equal nor deviant. Fundamentally pure, there is nothing to be obtained.

The wise clearly understand that there is nothing to be grasped; they do not rely on false pretenses, nor can they be said to be incapable of non-thought. Therefore, the wise do not take the various realms as their objective domain; these characteristics have no place of arising and exist only as conventional designations following worldly usage.
There is no conceptual discrimination because of the perception of non-arising; once this is extinguished, all realms cease to exist, existing only as provisional designations.
Having thoroughly investigated both the beginning and the end, they are entirely unknowable; that all things are likewise unknowable is what the wise perceive.
The Buddha said: “Dhāraṇīdhara!

If there is a bodhisattva who thoroughly understands this, comprehending the eighteen elements and the three realms, as well as the realm of sentient beings, the realm of one’s own body, and the realm of the space above—all of which they realize to be equal—then by contemplating them thus, they should respond with equanimity and not perceive any objective sphere. By having no such perceptions, they understand all realms; this is merely a provisional designation.”

"All realms are entirely devoid of realms; those who delight in entering the Way clearly understand all realms. Liberating sentient beings, their characteristics are non-dual; by perceiving this non-duality, they perceive all realms simultaneously. Through skillful means, they proclaim and demonstrate them to the multitude; the twelve links of dependent origination are merely provisional expressions used to transform and guide sentient beings toward the ultimate meaning. By fully manifesting the wisdom of insight into all realms, they are therefore called 'formless.'"
Why is this so? Dhāraṇīdhara!

The Tathāgata, the Arhat, does not find a location for any dharmas, yet it is not that he finds nothing at all; through non-forgetting and equanimous contemplation, he has attained the unsurpassed, right, and true path.

Why is this? Because all dharmas are eternally non-existent; from the very beginning they are all naturally so and have no achiever. All realms are empty; one perceives them as truly empty and non-existent. Since they are equal to space and possess no characteristic of arising, the Tathāgata understands all realms in this way.
The Tathāgata does not say that the various realms are spontaneously devoid of boundaries and form.
Why is this? That which is non-existent cannot be forcibly made to exist; because it is non-existent, one knows it to be spontaneous.

“Dhāraṇīdhara! You should know that regarding what the Tathāgata has taught: if there is one who understands the origin of all dharmas, that bodhisattva mahāsattva is then able to discern the beginning and end of the realms of all sentient beings. By understanding the beginning and end, they distinguish the coarse from the subtle, proclaiming the meaning of the convergence and dispersal of the various elements (*dhātu*). They understand that the entry into these various elements is not spontaneous; all elements are the realm of empty space. They are self-consuming, having neither element nor entry. Although they rely on provisional words, they can never be ultimately found. It is only because sentient beings lack knowledge that such things exist.”
It is like a master illusionist who has skillfully studied his art and manifests various transformations for the sake of sentient beings, displaying countless forms through these conjurations.
Those who do not understand cannot perceive that these are conjurations, and upon hearing or seeing them, they believe them to be truly existent;
yet those who clearly understand know that illusions are of their own nature.
The Buddha said: "It is so.

If one can clearly understand that sentient beings are illusory transformations, empty and non-existent, and are merely deceptive delusions; if one possesses clear wisdom and understands for oneself that one's own body is like an illusory transformation, realizing it to be a mere provisional attribution—then, regarding this world as such, one will naturally know it to be an illusion."

If there is a bodhisattva who understands and enters into this, who clarifies that illusions are spontaneous in order to liberate others through spontaneity, and who recognizes that the world in which one dwells is likewise like an illusion—then, through skillful means for the sake of sentient beings, they manifest and teach that all things are entirely like illusory transformations.

"If there are those who, upon hearing or seeing, understand that illusory phenomena are all non-existent, up to and including being truly real, yet the ignorant and deluded are unable to penetrate this, I therefore proclaim and expound all dharmas for their sake."

If one understands that all phenomena are entirely like illusions and wishes to enter into this meaning, one should train as follows: regarding the profound and essential Dharma, one does not seek to obtain form; because form is not obtained, it is not to be severed or eliminated. To speak of its non-severance and non-elimination is to say that all realms are merely provisional designations.

They manifest all combinations and disjunctions, distinguishing the various realms; they proclaim the causes and conditions created through expedient means and skillful methods; they analyze the fundamental roots and their ultimate ends to discern the True Truth (*satya*); they reveal the mundane and the supramundane, the conditioned and the unconditioned, the compliant and the non-compliant, and all that is appropriate or inappropriate. They proclaim the ultimate exhaustion of words through expedient means, and the causes and conditions elucidated through what is meaningful and what is meaningless. They speak of the distinction between places and placelessness, yet they realize that all these are like illusions.
Chapter Seven: The Bases of Cognition (*Āyatana*). In the *Dhṛtarāṣṭra-paripṛcchā-sūtra*, Chapter Seven: "The Bases of Cognition," the Buddha addressed Dhṛtarāṣṭra:
"What is meant by a bodhisattva’s thorough understanding of the bases of cognition?"
In this regard, the Bodhisattva contemplates the twelve bases (*āyatana*) and understands their beginning and end.
How does he contemplate them?
That which is contemplated is such that one does not perceive the locus of the eye-base; the eye is unestablished and entirely non-existent.
Why is this so? That which enters through the eye arises from the encounter of conditions and from inversion; it is bound by form and conjoined with dependent origination.
“There are two causal factors:
first, the sense-base of the eye;
second, the corresponding object.”

Because it rests upon form, it is called the eye-base (*cakṣur-āyatana*). Thus, there are two attachments regarding the eye and form: the entry of the eye into form, and form being the category of the eye. Having already perceived form through the gateway of illusion, they are therefore called the various bases (*āyatanas*).
Thus, when fullness arises and is received, the eye does not cling to forms, nor do forms cling to the eye; form does not cling to form, nor does the eye cling to the eye; all arise from conditions.

Because it takes form as its condition, it is called the "form base" (*rūpāyatana*). Because it itself encounters its conditions through seeing, it is said to possess characteristics; taking "entry" as its function.
What is meant by the function of entry?

Because they employ perversity, abundance, and suchness to the ultimate degree, they do not perceive the non-existence of forms that enter the eye; those of clear wisdom do not seek after the sense-bases and thus see the True Reality.
For foolish ordinary beings who are joined with inversion and immersed in darkness, there are two aspects.

When the eye encounters form, it manifests as entering into the truth; having understood that true reality, one realizes that form enters the eye, being neither internal, nor external, nor existing in between.

Regarding the eye, among all forms there is no past, future, or present; yet one perceives forms with the present eye. To perceive forms with the present eye and then greedily grasp them is the conduct of ignorant, deluded worldlings, which is not permissible.
The wise understand that emptiness has no reality; when thought becomes inverted, it forms the various sense bases (*āyatana*). Since these sense bases are spontaneous, how could they truly exist?
Their lack of the characteristic of being sense bases arises entirely from conditions; therefore, they are called "sense bases."

The Tathāgata said: "The various sense-bases (*āyatana*) are empty and non-existent; they all arise from inversion and depend upon causes and conditions. There is no agent and no one who causes action. The eye does not summon form, nor does form summon the eye; there is nothing that knows, for each is individually quiescent."

The eye and the various sense objects are both utterly tranquil; there is no agent, for they arise from causes and conditions. Ignorant and deluded ordinary people dwell in their minds in perversion, whereas the noble ones penetrate this truth: yet there is nothing produced and nothing extinguished!

“Without coming and without going, the eye and the various sense bases do not sever the continuity of the eye; the organ of sight does not conceptualize itself as ‘eye,’ and form does not abandon itself as ‘form’—thus one knows it to be spontaneous.”
One does not conceptualize form as form. Why is this?
Because each is empty, and because each is tranquil and known to be spontaneous.
The eye does not rely on the eye, nor does form know form, because they are of the nature of spontaneity (*svabhāva*).

Since the eye and form are spontaneous and lack any established entity, the eye does not seek the eye, nor do they join or disperse; each is empty and non-existent. The eye does not habituate itself to the thought "the eye is mine," nor does form habituate itself to the thought "form is mine. They are the spontaneous marks of illusion; that the eye and form are void and non-existent is called spontaneity—a term used as a provisional designation.
“Ear-sounds, nose-odors, tongue-tastes, body-touches, and mind-phenomena cannot be apprehended; they are all non-existent and have no establishment. Why is this?

Arising from causes and conditions, they abide in perversion and are established upon two causes; because various categories of mental phenomena arise and enter through them, they are called "entrances" (*āyatana*). By means of the causes and conditions of phenomena, one provisionally designates these as entrances.

Phenomena do not adhere to the mind, the mind does not adhere to phenomena, phenomena do not adhere to phenomena, and the mind does not adhere to the mind. Attachment arises from dependent origination and thereby establishes the affairs of phenomena; yet because one perceives signs through the mind, one cannot truly enter the Dharma—only the one of brilliant wisdom understands this.

"Seeking within the sense-bases (*āyatana*), one perceives the True Reality (*satya*): all are joined in inversion. Foolish and ignorant worldlings perceive two characteristics; yet there is neither internal nor external, nor is there anything in between. The mind does not enter phenomena, nor do phenomena enter the mind. There is no past, future, or present; all arise from conditions. The foolish do not understand this, but the wise comprehend it."

Why is this? Because all things are naturally non-existent; there is no entry into dharmas by means of the mind, nor is there any true characteristic, for nothing can be established—it is merely a provisional manifestation.
"In this way, Dhāraṇīdhara!

When a bodhisattva has attained such clear understanding of all these sense bases (āyatana), they comprehend all twelve sense bases; being neither attached nor bound, they sever the sense bases. By establishing and realizing the entry into them, they cause all conceptual discriminations to arise no more. They clearly understand the signless (animitta) to be like flowing water that merges wherever it meets!"
Therefore it is said that water is universal and there is nowhere it does not enter.

These twelve bases (*āyatana*) are likewise; what are called "internal" and "external" all arise from causes and conditions, and like the flow of water, they lead to the accomplishment of many things.

"Although it is said that spontaneity has no fixed location, because one perceives bondage and attachment, those who enter the various *āyatanas* head toward the gates of worldly toil (*kleśa*). Since ignorant and ordinary people do not sever this worldly toil, it is called 'entering the gates.'"
The eye is attached to forms; the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind are likewise so, having no place of resort.
The Bodhisattva Mahāsattva clearly understands the natural state and discerns the various sense bases (*āyatana*); having discerned these bases, he completely eliminates all fetters.
"In this way, Upāli, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva thoroughly understands the sense-bases. Chapter 8:
The Twelve Links of Dependent Origination From the *Upāliparipṛcchā-sūtra*, Chapter Eight: The Twelve Links of Dependent Origination. The Buddha addressed Upāli:
"What is meant by 'clearly understanding and proclaiming the various entrances'?
It is the contemplation of the twelve links of dependent origination.
By what means does one contemplate them?"
Because all phenomena are entirely the karma of ignorance, they are called "delusion" (moha);
because one does not understand that there is no locus [of existence], it is called "ignorance" (avidyā);
because one does not comprehend that the arising of all phenomena is itself ignorance, it is termed "delusion."
Because one does not understand, for what reason is there ignorance?

Because ignorance is the condition, there are volitional formations (*saṃskāra*). If one does not penetrate a phenomenon, one does not engage with that phenomenon; therefore, it is said that because ignorance is the condition, there are volitional formations.
Because there is the condition of volitional formations (*saṃskāra*), consciousness (*vijñāna*) arises; therefore, it is said that from volitional formations one reaches consciousness.
There are two aspects by which name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*) is brought about; therefore, from the condition of consciousness, name-and-form arises.
From name-and-form, the six sense bases arise; therefore it is said that conditioned by name-and-form, the six sense bases are attained.
Because there is contact, feeling arises; therefore it is said that conditioned by the six sense bases, contact arises.
Because there is feeling (vedanā), it is said that from the condition of contact (sparśa) feeling arises;
thus craving (tṛṣṇā) is produced, and so it is said that from the condition of feeling craving arises.
Because what is experienced arises from the condition of craving, it is said that "from the condition of craving, what is experienced arises.
Because possession arises from what is experienced, it is said that "from the condition of what is experienced, possession results."
From existence (*bhava*), birth arises; therefore it is said that with existence as condition, birth comes to be.

From the condition of birth, there arise aging, sickness, death, lamentation, sorrow, dejection, and distress—these great calamities and the meeting with suffering; therefore it is said that from birth come various forms of suffering.
"For what reason are these various afflictions combined?
It is because of ignorance (*avidyā*).

One practices various inversions; following the conduct of affection and love, one delights in and craves sensual desires. The mind, wherever it dwells, yearns for them and does not relinquish them. This is the mundane twelvefold dependent origination (*dvādaśāṅga-pratītyasamutpāda*), which is self-enclosed, blind and sightless, a net of ignorance, with the will fixed upon ulcers and leprosy, entering into profound darkness."
With ignorance as the foremost, one contemplates the twelve links of dependent origination in this way, thereby realizing that this ignorance is deceptive and not real;
furthermore, its ultimate origin cannot be known.
Why is it unknowable?
Because it is unknowable, one does not attain clarity.
Due to ignorance (*avidyā*), the original limit of its arising is unknowable.

If one possesses clear wisdom, they should observe this: by understanding the original limit (*pūrvakoṭi*), one reaches the limitlessness; thus, neither giving rise to conceptual thought nor dwelling in non-conceptualization, one severs all perceptions.
By severing all conceptualizations, one does not rely upon ignorance; yet, all dharmas do not conflict with ignorance.
These dharmas do not depart from the conceited mind of ignorance.
Why is this so? Because one abandons ignorance, it is said that all dharmas are called ignorance.

One who is able to realize that all dharmas are ignorance attains the activity of clarity (*vidyā-karman*) and no longer seeks further clarity; because this extinguishes ignorance, it is called the activity of clarity.

"What is meant by 'extinguishing ignorance'? It means understanding that all phenomena are entirely non-existent; that all dharmas are empty and unreal; that they exist only within the state of inversion and lack any inherent existence, being merely provisional designations."
This is what is called severing ignorance (*avidyā*) and also severing the presence of knowledge (*vidyā*).

Both knowledge and ignorance are entirely empty and unreal. That which is called ignorance gives rise to various karmic activities through the functioning of ignorance, thereby resulting in the twelve links [of dependent origination]. Foolish, ignorant worldlings cannot penetrate this; they cast themselves into false darkness, taking that which is utterly non-existent to be existent, and thus it is called "volitional formations" (*saṃskāra*).

There is no place, no speech, no speaking, and no knowing; clarity is neither bright nor dark. All karmic activities of the various formations (*saṃskāra*) are fundamentally empty and non-existent; among all dharmas, there is no such thing as a contrary action toward what exists. Therefore, it is said that the condition of ignorance (*avidyā*) brings about the formation of all volitional actions.
"Those formations are impermanent; they arise from various non-virtuous karmas.
Furthermore, when one examines these formations, they are found to be without past, future, or present; their ignorance is empty, and one should discern that ignorance."

All conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) are fundamentally empty, and all phenomena are spontaneously so (*svabhāva*). Phenomena have no point of attachment; it is because of ignorance (*avidyā*) that conditioned phenomena arise. That ignorance does not attach itself to the phenomena; when the continuity of ignorance is severed through clear knowledge (*vidyā*), ignorance is then extinguished. One does not eliminate phenomena by means of phenomena; rather, these phenomena, when accompanied by ignorance, give rise to darkness and obscuration. When one abides in inversion and ignorance cannot be apprehended, this is called spontaneous non-apprehension of phenomena, which is also called spontaneity (*svabhāva*).
Because it uses the darkness of obscurity as its obstruction, it is called ignorance (*avidyā*); because one employs this obscure ignorance, formations (*saṃskāra*) are established.

"If a phenomenon were without ignorance and non-existent, then through deceptive phenomena, ignorance would be formed; yet in the formation of consciousness, one forms without attachment, and does not give rise to the formation of consciousness."
Why is this so? Practice does not know practice;
in practice there is no dharma that can be reached or attained. From practice and consciousness, various inversions arise.
This practice and consciousness have no interior, no exterior, and no middle. There is no one who gives rise to consciousness; it is simply because practice is dissipated that consciousness arises.

If that wise person seeks consciousness and does not find it—seeing that consciousness has no place of origin and nothing to be seen—and does not differentiate it from name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*), the six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*), contact (*sparśa*), feeling (*vedanā*), craving (*tṛṣṇā*), becoming (*bhava*), birth (*jāti*), and old age, sickness, death, grief, lamentation, pain, and distress—the great mass of suffering (*duḥkhaskandha*)—then they will not revolve in the boundless cycle of birth and death nor remain unable to save themselves amidst the five rivers and four streams.

To clearly understand that there are no roots and that all things are entirely without attachment, and to achieve the karma of the ultimate equality, one contemplates the twelve links of dependent origination in this same way; this is called the clarity of non-duality. Therefore, one diligently exerts oneself to seek all dharmas, yearning for those dharmas as being neither conceptualized nor non-conceptualized; this is the compliant clarity of entering the twelve links of dependent origination.
"Thus it is, Dhāraṇīdhara!

When the assembly of bodhisattvas clearly understands and proclaims that the twelve links of dependent origination arise through the conjunction of conditions, yet discerns them as being without such conjunction, this is called attaining the liberation of non-arising. To clearly understand dependent origination and contemplate the twelve links, one should not examine their arising nor fall into the wisdom of expedient means regarding non-arrival."

If one can thoroughly understand that the twelve links of dependent origination (*dvādaśāṅga-pratītyasamutpāda*) are without arising, this is called being fully awakened to and attaining the wisdom of non-arising (*anutpāda-jñāna*). "Therefore, Upālī!

A Bodhisattva Mahāsattva who wishes to enter the wisdom of non-arising and establish its realization should analyze and expound the twelve links of dependent origination and practice them. By practicing otherwise regarding all links of dependent origination as being without arising, and by forming this contemplation, one is said to have attained the wisdom of non-arising. Because one is able to attain the wisdom of non-arising and establish its realization, it is called attaining the awakened understanding of the path-wisdom of non-origination (*anutpāda-mārga-jñāna*)."

"Therefore, Upāli! When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices in this way, although there are conditions from which they arise, there is no actual arising; they completely sever the three realms and, through the realization of dependent origination, they contemplate that nothing arises."

If there are bodhisattvas who reach the mark of non-arising, they will swiftly attain the forbearance toward the non-arising of dharmas (anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti). They will immediately draw near to the practice of a bodhisattva; having personally attended upon and faced the various Buddhas, they receive the prediction of enlightenment (vyākaraṇa). They shall attain the unsurpassed, right, and true path to become the most perfectly awakened ones (anuttara-samyak-saṃbuddha); having received this prediction before long, they draw near to its actualization.

Furthermore, by manifesting such physical forms themselves and practicing the Buddha's teachings, these true men each receive their prediction of enlightenment and attain the joy of faith; they discern all phenomena of the world to deliver beings according to their various customs.

Having clearly understood the root of the twelve links of dependent origination and thereby attained realization of dependent origination, the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, stand manifest before one's eyes, and one no longer fears the Māra Pāpīyān.

If one perceives all things on land and in water in the present, beholding birth and death, having crossed over all calamities and uprooted the source of ignorance, then through such analogies one shall forever attain peace and security, beholding the True Person.
The Buddha said, “Dhāraṇīdhara!

If there is a bodhisattva who understands in this way that all which belongs to the self exists because of causes and conditions, and who, upon hearing this, comprehends the beginning and end of the twelve links of dependent origination, believing and rejoicing without doubt, then they have established the root-source of all Tathāgatas. Before long, they will receive the prediction of enlightenment and attain the patience regarding the non-arising of phenomena (anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti). Because they have received the prediction, the Tathāgatas will not be far away; the Tathāgatas will then grant them the decision for the Way, and they shall reach the unsurpassed, right, and true path to become a Most Perfectly Awakened One.”
The Sūtra of the Bodhisattva Dhāraṇīdhara, Scroll Two.
The Sūtra of the Bodhisattva Dhāraṇīdhara, Scroll Three.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Zhu Fahu of the Yuezhi during the Western Jin Dynasty.
Chapter Nine: The Thirty-Seven Factors of Enlightenment.
The Buddha addressed the Bodhisattva Dhāraṇīdhara:
“What is meant by a bodhisattva’s clear understanding of the applications of mindfulness?”
If there is a bodhisattva who, through analytical observation, practices the four foundations of mindfulness—what are these four foundations?
He observes his own body; he likewise observes sensation, perception, and mental phenomena in the same way.
"What is meant by observing for oneself feelings, perceptions, and mental phenomena?

In this regard, the bodhisattva observes his own bodily conduct as it truly is, [realizing] that impermanence, suffering, emptiness, and non-self are its essentials; that the body is a wound and a disease, fraught with peril and manifold harms, which one habitually takes for pleasure, yet is flickering, transitory, and impure."
Contemplating in this way, one sees that various defects fill this body; from the nine types of orifices, impurities flow out day and night, its foul and unclean state being like that of a latrine.

Contemplate this thus: there is not even so much as a hair’s breadth that can be found pleasant or worth grasping. Impure and turbid, skin covers the flesh; sinews bind it together, formed through the accumulation of merit and demerit. Through the gathering of manifold attachments, the "aggregates" (skandhas) come into being.
What is meant by "accumulation" (upadhi)?
What is meant by "aggregates" (skandha)?

These aggregates all exist due to conditions from past lives; because one fundamentally relies upon and yearns for them, they are covered by falsehoods. One bathes and adorns them, claiming, "This is my body," and it is through this that accumulation occurs.
"What is meant by the 'aggregates of flourishing' (skandhas)?

They arise from causes and conditions and are formed through retribution; they evolve from the performance of karmic formations based on the four great elements. When one calculates the beginning and end of the body, it is seen that it is not a truly existent thing."
Receiving the four great elements, one forms the aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*), thereby obtaining a provisional basis for designation.
Why is it called "body" (*kāya*)?
Because it has been self-constructed, it is called the body.
Because the mind relies upon it, it is called the body;
because it is that wherein transgressions and blessings are produced, it is called the body.
Because it gives rise from thought to what is unworthy and contemptible, and because it accords with karmic action, it is called the body.

The body is formed from causes and conditions; it attains a slight measure of peace only to fall into decay again, unable to endure for long. It cannot remain forever but must soon be parted from; therefore, it is called "the body."

"There is no interior, no exterior, and no middle. Although it is established as a state of oppression and affliction, the body does not know the body, nor can it be seen; it is not clarified by understanding, nor can it reach the further shore. It is devoid of thought, like grass, trees, tiles, or stones; the body does not constitute a body."

By practicing such contemplation and establishing this understanding and penetration, one does not crave the body and has no longing for its pleasures; one knows that the body is a source of affliction. The body has no past, future, or present; what is not the body is treated as the body, like a mass of foam. To bathe and adorn it is like treating a house [as one's own];
within this body dwell eighty kinds of worms, which cause oppression and distress;
there are hundreds of countless diseases, and this body is without rescue, beset by the tribulations of the three sufferings.
That which is called suffering refers to the afflictions of birth and death and the hardships of separation; this body is a vessel of suffering that undergoes all manner of perils and calamities.
By contemplating in this way and reflecting on the meaning of compliance with truth, one will not crave the body, will not long for others, and will have no objects of desire or pleasure.

This body is without self; though it exists, it is subject to separation. The body has no possession and is entirely devoid of reality. This body is empty by its very nature and inherently void; it reaches the ultimate non-existence, being established merely as a true falsehood. Its fetters are useless, having been formed through the practices of the beginningless past.
Although one possesses this body, it is not one's own body; one should rouse single-minded diligence and seek non-attachment.

Having been able to observe that one's own body and lifespan cannot be found to either combine or disperse, nor can their coming, going, or place of abiding be seen, nor can the past, future, or present be perceived—one who is without thought or non-thought is entirely without attachment. Not relying on body or life, the body is not "mine," nor is there anything belonging to me; thus, there is nothing to be grasped.

Neither conjoined nor dispersed, it comes from nowhere; it causes the mind to be distressed and feverish, such that its destination is unknown. When one calculates the beginning and end of the body, there is nothing that arises, is born, abides, stands, ceases, or is extinguished.

“The Bodhisattva contemplates the body in this way as being bodiless; having realized the emptiness of the body, whenever desire for the body arises, it is immediately extinguished. Thus, the intention regarding the body ceases, and one abides in accordance with the practice; by contemplating the body according to its true meaning, there is simply no body.”
The Buddha told Dhāraṇīdhara:
"What is meant by a bodhisattva contemplating the sensations of the body?
If there is a bodhisattva who examines the three types of bodily sensation:"
There are pleasant sensations, painful sensations, and sensations that are neither pleasant nor painful.

When one calculates these sensations and their itching-like fluctuations, one finds no destination from which they come; they neither depart nor arrive, but arise solely from emptiness. They are formed through the conjunction of causes and conditions as one receives the retribution of sins and blessings, originating from inverted views.

One knows that sensation is fundamentally non-existent, established only through conceptualization. One who practices this contemplation does not perceive pleasure or pain; there is no past, future, or present, nor is any location perceived.
Regarding past sensations, one realizes they are empty, without self, and without what belongs to a self; they are impermanent, lacking solidity, and entirely inverted phenomena.

Past sensations are empty, tranquil, and devoid of perception; the future and the present are likewise so. Thus one knows that sensations cannot be established; they have no form to be grasped and each disintegrates on its own.

These sensations of pain and pleasure have no originator, nor do they cease; they have no location, being neither internal nor external. It is through the inversion of perception that ignorant and ordinary people give rise to these sensations. When the retribution for their transgressions and merits is exhausted, they are accordingly separated from them; therefore, it is said that all sensations are empty, insubstantial, and deceptive phenomena.

"By such knowledge, one understands that the mind finds its locus through the condition of feeling; yet when feeling comes to an end, it must necessarily return to extinction, for one does not perceive any place where feeling and sensation aggregate."
The mind thought to itself:
"Sensation is empty; it is naturally formless and its arising cannot be seen.
Sensation has no place of origin, nor does it have cessation, nor is there any perception of its formation."
"Because there is no perception of existence, there is no characteristic;
since characteristics do not arise, one contemplates thus universally, such that the sensations of pain and itching within the body have nothing upon which to rely."

Understanding that the true reality of sensation is fundamentally non-existent, one cuts off sensation and departs from all sensory bases; not uniting with them and not clinging to sensation, all conditioned activities become tranquil as one swiftly seeks skillful means and attains samādhi-concentration.
When a bodhisattva examines the activity of sensation in this way, seeing that activity through full understanding, they behold the ten directions.
The Buddha told Dhāraṇīdhara:
“What is meant by a bodhisattva observing the mental activities of the mind?”

If there is a bodhisattva who contemplates the movements of mental activity and, in the brief moment a thought arises, examines the mental phenomena, and if they are able to observe them even as various transformations occur, that mind will think to itself:
"This mind has never run wild, nor has it reached anywhere."

The characteristics toward which one is driven by various conditions are dispelled; that which the mind arouses is likewise not established. It has no form or appearance and is entirely ungraspable; the mind neither comes nor goes and stands nowhere. It is without past, future, or present, yet it gives rise to thoughts through the manifestation of causes and conditions.

When the mind calculates this, there is nothing internal, nothing external, and no intermediate state that can cause oppression or affliction; the mind has no location and is not of a spontaneous nature!
It cannot be brought into being, and the mind has nothing to be severed.
If there is anything to be severed, the mind is termed "various transformations," which are incalculable; as soon as the characteristic of arising appears, it is extinguished. "Dhāraṇīdhara!
The mind has no place of abiding and no place of persistence; having already awakened to its location, this is then a state where there is neither mental ideation nor anything seen."
Why is this so? Furthermore, that mind is empty and spontaneous, formless and devoid of sentient beings; moreover, it possesses nothing and finds no location.
There is no one who unites the mind, nor anyone who disperses it; the mind has no past, no future, and no middle can be found.

There is no one who can see it; the mind does not arise spontaneously, the mind is not impure, the mind does not know the mind, and the mind is never severed. When the mind has no mind, it is called primordial purity (*prakṛti-viśuddhi*).

“Ordinary worldlings, dwelling in perversion and ignorant darkness, are taught by means of false causes and conditions regarding various marks; thus their minds spontaneously give rise to such thoughts.

Furthermore, although that mind is empty and devoid of a self, they reckon it to possess a body and mind, existing as permanent, eternal, and forever secure; through these perverted dharmas, they cast themselves into the darkness.”
Observing the mind in this way, one attains the mental stillness of pliancy.
The mind has neither conceptualization nor non-conceptualization; having clearly understood this mind, one forms no notion of "arising" regarding that which arises.
Why is this so? Because the mind has no arising, it cannot attain the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*); since its characteristics cannot be attained, the characteristics of the mind do not arise.

The wise understand and penetrate this through discernment; they know that what the mind habituates and pursues returns to cessation. They clearly know that as it truly is: when one thus observes the mind, there is no habitual association, no cessation, and no place of return, because the mind cannot be apprehended.
If one cannot even attain the mind, how much less can one attain the ultimate state of what is practiced and what is sought?
For this reason, the mind does not conceive of extinction, nor does it dwell in non-conceptuality, thereby attaining purity of mind;
once the mind is pure, it does not follow after worldly afflictions and is not defiled by them.

Why is this so? Because one knows that when all mental states are removed, the mind becomes pure; when the minds of sentient beings are distracted, they become defiled by worldly afflictions (*kleśa*). When the mind is pure, it is pure precisely because one is able to know how to remove [distractions].
He thought to himself:

"The mind possesses afflictions; for this reason, one calculates the conduct of sentient beings. When the mind has attachments, it constitutes affliction; when the mind is liberated through clarity, it attains purity."

Having performed this contemplation, one neither attains a mind attached to the dust of desire nor attains a pure mind; only then does one fully realize that the fundamental nature of the mind is intrinsically pure.
When a bodhisattva contemplates the activities of the mind and mental factors in this way, they immediately penetrate their original purity.
The Buddha told Dhāraṇīdhara:

“What is meant by a bodhisattva’s mind abiding in the Dharma and contemplating the practice of that Dharma? If there is a bodhisattva who contemplates all dharmas, seeing neither internal dharmas nor external dharmas, nor dwelling in between; if they encounter affliction, they realize that dharmas have no past, future, or present. They arise through the twelve links of dependent origination, and among these inverted dharmas, there is no true accomplishment.”

"Furthermore, when examining these dharmas, they have neither interior nor exterior, nor do they have a middle. Dharmas neither aggregate nor disperse; all dharmas are entirely without form or appearance. They neither exist nor do they not exist; they are merely based upon sounds."
All phenomena are like empty space and like illusory manifestations; they arise naturally as fundamentally pure and luminous, yet each has its own attachments and labors.
All phenomena are invisible; when one examines their reality, they are like what is seen in a dream, which upon awakening is no longer seen.
All dharmas are like reflected images; they are fundamentally pure, formless, and beyond names and concepts, for all dharmas are without thought.
All dharmas are like echoes produced by calling; since they arise from emptiness, these dharmas are non-existent, and because they are spontaneous, they cannot be apprehended.
"All dharmas are like a mirage because they do not exist.

One who can contemplate all dharmas by establishing them as such sees various transformations; yet, one knows that there are no dharmas and that non-dharmas neither join nor disperse, thereby seeing that all dharmas are forever without attachment."
By performing this contemplation, one sees that all phenomena neither go nor return, and does not perceive any established locus for phenomena.

Why is this? Because there is neither a locus nor a non-locus; all phenomena arise from causes and conditions, abiding within the boundless cycle of inversion. They are beyond speech and non-speech, free from dualistic conceptions, yet they are not a single conception, nor do they possess a minor conception. This is what the enlightened understand, yet it cannot be apprehended; nor is it that it is not apprehended.
Why is this? All dharmas are neither born nor do they arise;
they are without creation or action, and no agent can be found. All dharmas relinquish form and possess no physical appearance, yet they are spontaneously accomplished through spontaneity itself!

Because all dharmas are fundamentally the ineffable ultimate truth, one who contemplates in this way understands that all dharmas are without self, without person, and without life-force. Examining their emptiness and non-existence, the mind reflects:
"All dharmas are by nature empty; since dharmas are spontaneous, they are also devoid of conceptualization. One does not perceive manifold conceptions and does not create aspirations for dharmas."

Observing all phenomena as being without arising, he thought to himself: "Phenomena neither arise nor cease. By contemplating in this way, he attained the application of mindfulness regarding phenomena (*dharmasmṛtyupasthāna*).

He realized that all phenomena are fundamentally without arising; he understood that they return to the exhaustion of habitual tendencies and are established through the characteristics of causes and conditions. Being naturally detached from them, they are devoid of marks.
Why is this so? Because there is no formation; that which is signless is simply the relinquishing of signs.
Those who are wise and discerning realize and awaken to the fact that all these dharmas are fundamentally non-existent.

“If there is a bodhisattva who should contemplate the dharma-practice of all dharmas in this way, by performing such practice, they do not apprehend any dharmas nor is there anything produced; they do not give rise to any dharmas that abide or cease, for all dharmas possess the characteristic of parinirvāṇa—the characteristics of the faculties are quiescent and their characteristics are likewise tranquil.”

When a bodhisattva contemplates all phenomena in this way, they fully comprehend the application of mindfulness to phenomena (*dharmasmṛtyupasthāna*). Having no place of abiding and nothing in which not to abide, they enter entirely into the characteristic of the luminous wisdom of all phenomena. By examining their own mental reflections and attaining the application of mindfulness to phenomena, this is called the proclamation of the sūtras.

To abide nowhere among all phenomena, to expound all dharmas by using wisdom to subdue delusion—this is called beholding the ultimate truth within all phenomena and attaining the station of mindfulness regarding the Dharma.
The Buddha said:

"When the mind is stilled, one then reaches the abandonment of the mind. Regarding the body, feelings, perceptions, and mental formations, by understanding that the three realms are empty and not perceiving the body, feelings, perceptions, or mental formations, one achieves the four abandonments of the mind."
The Buddha told Dhāraṇīdhara:
"If a bodhisattva attains understanding of the five faculties and transcends the root of the mundane world, they should examine them in accordance with the truths.
What are these five faculties?
First is the faculty of faith, second is the faculty of diligence, third is the faculty of intention, fourth is the faculty of concentration, and fifth is the faculty of wisdom;
these are the five faculties, and one should observe their practice.
How does one contemplate this?

One believes that all phenomena arise from causes and conditions; they are established through the combination of inverted and empty states, revolving incessantly and without fixedness like a wheel, wandering without limit, and like a dream, naturally vanishing away.

One should believe that all phenomena are impermanent, suffering, empty, and non-self; that sickness, sores, and old age do not endure, and that nothing can remain for long, as one must inevitably part from it again.
All phenomena are unreal and lack any substantiality; they are but fleeting illusions, like the scattering and release of the various sense faculties.
It is like a painted image or the strength of a small child; one’s thoughts and delusions take what is false for reality, not knowing that it is all deceptive and utterly non-existent.

As for the faculty of faith: all dharmas have no past, future, or present; they neither go nor come, nor do they abide anywhere. They are empty, signless, and wishless; without arising or activity; without conceptualization and without delusion. Their morality is pure, their concentration is pure, and their wisdom, liberation, and the aggregate of knowledge and vision are pure.
One who is able to uphold this practice of the faculty of faith shall not turn back.

Taking sincere faith as the foremost, they establish the prohibitive precepts, remaining entirely without loss and never deviating from the work of the Path. Because there is no loss, they accord with the True Dharma and abide in sincere faith, incapable of being shaken.

When one is moved by the retribution of virtuous merit to come and receive protection, one establishes upright karma free from flattery and cuts off all sixty-two types of false views and conditions. One does not seek external teachings to serve as a master; it is like seeing the sun and moon and having no need for a torch. One takes refuge only in the Tathāgata and recognizes the assembly of noble ones, fully perfecting pure karma through precepts, patience, gentleness, and harmony. Thus, with firm faith that is unshakable—possessing an indestructible and profound sense of righteous faith—one then becomes endowed with the Dharma.
The Buddha told Dhāraṇīdhara:
"What is meant by a bodhisattva contemplating the faculty of diligence?
How does one fully accomplish and master skillful means?"

If there is a bodhisattva who is steadfast in the Way and does not deviate from it, who, through diligence, puts an end to the five hindrances; and who, having had the opportunity to hear such profound and wondrous scriptures as these, zealously and compliantly practices them; who exerts themselves day and night without becoming despondent or weak; whose mind does not forget its far-reaching resolve and who yearns for extensive learning and unobstructed dharmas; and who, by severing all obscurations, does not abandon their diligence.

If a thought of evil or unwholesome dharmas arises in the mind, one eliminates it through great diligence; having recognized that a dharma has arisen, one establishes diligent cultivation without ever becoming weary, practicing with unremitting diligence and applying oneself with focused effort, never failing in this practice, nor retreating from the exertion of the power one follows.

Thoroughly understanding all phenomena and discerning them as they truly are, one does not look up to others for support; remaining steadfast in the governance of the world without losing diligence, one possesses the greatest majesty and virtue through this faculty of vigor (*vīryendriya*). By diligently studying according to the Dharma, one attains the designation of the faculty of vigor.
The Buddha told Dhāraṇīdhara:
"What is meant by a bodhisattva attaining mastery over the faculty of mind?
How does one clearly understand and practice the faculty of mind?"

If there is a bodhisattva who restrains their mind, practicing in accordance with generosity, precepts, and learning, and being fully endowed with pure conduct (*brahmacarya*), they perfect the categories of purity in the precepts, concentration, wisdom, liberation, and the knowledge and vision of liberation; they purify body, speech, and mind, ultimately becoming humble and respectful as they establish right intention; they abide in all dharmas without giving rise to [dualistic] birth, dwelling in distinction while observing ultimate practice; they eliminate suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path; they maintain the establishment of the foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*); through skillful means, they penetrate and understand the faculties (*indriya*), powers (*bala*), factors of awakening (*bodhyaṅga*), and the one-pointedness of mind (*ekāgratā*)—the samādhi of right reception; they comprehend all dharmas without conceptualization or aspiration, attaining non-arising wisdom and reaching noble patience; they depart from desire and attain extinction (*nirvāṇa*) through the attainment of mental stillness, becoming fully endowed with the Buddha-dharmas and not proceeding to the stages of the śrāvaka or pratyekabuddha.

Revering unimpeded wisdom, his mind is not deluded; by being able to apply himself single-mindedly to such a dharma as this, he is prudent in body and speech, does not lose his intent, and does not rely on others. Examining such a dharma, he possesses the greatest majesty and virtue, attaining the fundamental source; this is called understanding thoroughly and attaining the faculty of concentration.
"What is meant by a bodhisattva attaining the faculty of concentration?
How does one clearly understand this faculty of concentration?

If there is a bodhisattva who practices meditative reflection with single-mindedness and without falsehood, performing the deeds of the noble ones with a meditative mind free from attachment, and through non-negligent meditation skillfully gathering the faculty of concentration; if they clearly comprehend and perfectly understand the faculty of concentration, and through non-perverted meditation contemplate the gateway of concentration, thereby achieving an unconfused state and entering into tranquil resolve."

Arising from samādhi, he no longer dwells in fixed concentration nor experiences formal meditative attainment (*samāpatti*); yet, because he aspires to and delights in establishing himself in the path of practice, he finds joy through the cultivation of dhyāna and reflection, needing no longer to rely on others. His dhyāna and meditative attainments do not follow the mere teachings on dhyāna; having reached majestic virtue, a concentrated mind, and single-mindedness, he does not crave gain or offerings and conducts himself without turmoil. By means of this supreme majestic virtue, he attains the faculty of mental concentration, reaching the *pāramitā* of deliverance.
The Buddha told Dhāraṇīdhara:
"What is called the bodhisattva’s practice of the faculty of wisdom?
How does one clearly understand and attain the faculty of wisdom?"
If there is a bodhisattva who extinguishes the activities of the body, what does this mean?

It means to completely eliminate all suffering and constantly dissolve bodily activities; wherever one practices wisdom, one universally perceives the departure from desire, extinguishing habitual tendencies and exhausting the path toward the gate of the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*). By practicing the faculty of wisdom, one beholds all within the three realms as ablaze and knows the suffering of the three realms.

Those who possess wisdom do not rely upon the triple world; they examine it and see it all as empty, signless, and wishless. Their minds give rise to nothing and no longer engage in further activity; those who perceive this completely relinquish all conditioned phenomena.
As if their heads were on fire, they shall fulfill the Buddha-dharma and single-mindedly practice all dharmas.
Although they dwell within the triple world, they suppress and extinguish everything, completely relinquishing all attachments, and thus have no longing for anything within the triple world.
He has severed all that is cherished and abandoned all conditioned phenomena; free from all defiled bonds of craving and fetters, his mind is without attachment.
He does not long for the five pleasures, nor does he cling to the realms of desire, form, or formlessness.
The mind harbors the merit of sagely wisdom and brilliance, which is immeasurable like the rivers and seas; its practice of utmost sincerity has no limit or bottom.

Understanding all phenomena, one uses wisdom to discern that the triple world is entirely without attachment; this is the supreme virtue and righteousness, revering wisdom and attaining the boundless liberation.
The Buddha said,
“Dhāraṇīdhara!
For what reason are they called ‘roots’ (indriya)?”
That which is called a "root" (mūla) is so named because its nature is immovable; thus it is called a root.
Because it is without movement and without dissipation or flight, it is called a root.
Because it never turns back and does not rely upon or look up to others, and because its nature is without companion as it accords with and follows the Dharma-teaching, it is called a root.
That which others cannot shame and which nothing can shake is unmixed and unconfused; therefore, it is called the "root.
Thus, O Upholder!
This is how a bodhisattva thoroughly understands all faculties.
"Furthermore, Dhāraṇīdhara!
A bodhisattva discerns the faculties of sentient beings and is well-trained in the Vaipulya sūtras.

He knows which roots of sentient beings are defiled and which are undefiled; he knows those with the faculty of desire and those without the faculty of desire; he knows those with the faculty of anger and those without the faculty of anger; and he knows those with the faculty of delusion and those without the faculty of delusion."

He knows the faculties of those who have fallen into the evil realms or those born among humans; he knows the faculties of those born in the heavens before the Buddhas of the ten directions; and whether their minds are sharp, dull, or intermediate, he perceives and knows them all clearly.
He fully knows those of base and coarse faculties, as well as those whose faculties are incomplete; he also knows those whose faculties are unimpaired.
He further knows those whose faculties accord with the Dharma, those who possess skillful means, and those who lack skillful means.
One should fully know the roots of guilt and the roots of innocence; the roots of attachment and the roots of non-attachment; the roots of harm and the roots of non-harm.

One should be able to know the roots that are conformable and the roots that are non-conformable; the roots that are obstructed and the roots that are unobstructed; the roots of the desire realm, the roots of the form realm, and the roots of the formless realm; as well as the roots that bring forth all virtues and the roots of ultimate goodness.

He fully knows the faculties that lead to various destinies, the faculty of gentleness and harmony, the faculty of dwelling in false views, the faculty of establishing right views, the faculty of stinginess and greed, and the faculty of being free from stinginess and avarice.

He fully knows the faculty of violence and the faculty of non-violence; the faculty of delusion and the faculty of non-delusion; the faculty of haste and the faculty of gentleness; the faculty of patience and the faculty of anger; the faculty of harboring envy and the faculty of being without envy; the faculty of practicing generosity and the faculty of not practicing generosity; the faculty of faith and the faculty of lack of faith; the faculty of desire and the faculty of detachment from desire; the faculty of household life and the faculty of renouncing the household life; and the faculty of perfecting precepts and the faculty of violating precepts. He knows them all.

He fully knows the faculty of restraint, the faculty of non-restraint, the faculty of purity, the faculty of patience, the faculty of malice and resentment, the faculty of supreme diligence, the faculty of indolence, the faculty of a distracted mind, the faculty of grasping at essentials, the faculty of concentrated mind, the faculty of wisdom, the faculty of lost wisdom, the faculty of possessing noble clarity, the faculty of folly, the faculty of fearlessness, the faculty of arrogance, the faculty of being free from arrogance, the faculty of having attained the Path, the faculty of following false views, the faculty of a peaceful and harmonious mind, and the faculty of a dissolute and unrestrained mind.

The faculty of dispersion, the faculty of tranquility, the faculty of arising, the faculty of non-arising, the faculty of purity, the faculty of defilement, the faculty of understanding and illumination, the faculty of radiance, the faculty of the śrāvaka, the faculty of the pratyekabuddha, the faculty of the bodhisattva vehicle, and the faculty of the buddha vehicle—one thoroughly understands and attains them all; this is called "attaining power."
Being without equal and free from negligence—meaning that one does not turn back but attains skillful means—is called the faculty of mind (*manendriya*).

It knows the faculties of devas, nāgas, yakṣas, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, mahoragas, humans, and non-humans; it is most majestic and honored, invincible and unshakable. Its practiced skillful means universally save beings to the utmost degree. By reverently practicing and diligently cultivating such scriptures as these, one swiftly attains clear understanding and achieves mastery over all phenomena, circulating through the worlds of the ten directions, saving all without exception.
The Buddha told Dhāraṇīdhara:
"What is meant by a bodhisattva’s thorough understanding of the Way?
How does one attain the Way?"
If there is a bodhisattva who upholds the Eightfold Noble Path:
first, right view; second, right mindfulness; third, right speech; fourth, right livelihood; fifth, right action; sixth, right effort; seventh, right intention; and eighth, right concentration.
"What is called right view?
It is when a bodhisattva eliminates all false views. Why is this so?"
Regarding all that is seen, from the mundane up to Nirvana—if one wishes to see the Buddha, one must eliminate all such karmic activities of seeing; this is called right view (*samyag-dṛṣṭi*).

By being without seeing and not accepting views, one establishes what is called "all views. Being entirely without reliance and universally without conceptualization, and by being without inversion and without non-conceptualization, this is called right view.
What is meant by "the equality of what is seen"?

It means to abandon worldly falsehoods and discard deviant views; to eliminate all that is perceived through suchness-seeing; to abide in right view without any attachment; to neither conceive nor not conceive, and thus not perceive nirvāṇa; to distance oneself from all views of desire and not to practice any views.
"What is called right view?

It is the state where all things are tranquil, unborn, and cool, and wherein there is also nothing to be extinguished; it is the equal contemplation of the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*). Being fundamentally pure, one has no expectations regarding any phenomena, yet there is neither non-thought nor anything to which one does not respond. This is called the right view that transcends the world."

"What is called right view? It does not grasp at the present, nor does it transcend the world. Right view severs both worldly dharmas and that which transcends the world; it does not conceive of the present or the transcendent, but eliminates all conceptions. It does not attain to equality or inequality, but severs all practices of equality. This is called transcending the world, and this is termed right view."
All such things are entirely without arising; therefore, it is called right view.
To see the true reality as it is, with right view free from error—this is called right view.
Thus it is, O Dhāraṇīdhara!
This is the right view practiced by Bodhisattva Mahāsattvas.
What is meant by right mindfulness?
It is to understand all objects of thought according to the ultimate truth—that they are all false conceptions—and to contemplate the unconditioned Buddha, Dharma, and Noble Sangha.

Why is this so? Because it severs all conceptualizations and thoughts into equality; it is right mindfulness (*samyak-smṛti*) because of this mindfulness. To be without manifold marks is called right mindfulness. Why is this so?

To eliminate all conceptualization is called "examining correctly"; thus, there is no more deviation and one no longer harbors thoughts. One then abides in right mindfulness and does not grasp at what is conceived; because one is free from both deviant and correct conceptualization, it is called "right mindfulness."

By eliminating perceptions and discarding all mental proliferations, abandoning false inversions, and dissolving both thought and non-thought, one equanimously regards all thoughts; by not clinging to any thoughts and eliminating all perceptions, it is called right mindfulness (*samyak-smṛti*).
"What is meant by right speech?

All verbal expressions are false; they exist within inversion and consist entirely of delusive conceptions. Seeing equality, one reflects in the mind upon speech and correctly cuts off all that is proclaimed through verbal expression; therefore, it is called right speech."

Speech has no point of convergence; it neither departs nor arrives. What is perceived is thus, equal and without distinction. Having attained right speech, all that is proclaimed by the mouth is true and sincere; therefore, it is called right speech.

Their speech is pure; in whatever place they dwell, they sever all verbal teachings and eloquence. With mental awakening, their mouths have nothing to proclaim; they completely abandon deviant speech and abide in right speech.
"What is called right action?
By abiding in right action, one knows that all various wrong actions are neither true nor real, for fundamentally nothing has been done."
Why is this so? Because all karmas have no ultimate end; since karma is entirely dispersed, it is called right action (*samyak-karmānta*).

It is neither in the right nor in the wrong, neither in "is" nor in "is not. Without perception or non-perception, one transcends all karmas. By not creating right or wrong, and so forth, one attains the state where all karmas are neither performed nor unperformed; therefore, it is called right action.

They are all able to equally expound upon the various karmas of the heterodox and the orthodox; as they understand all karmas according to ultimate truth (paramārtha-satya), they also see through ultimate truth that there is neither what is appropriate nor what is inappropriate—this is called right action (samyak-karmānta).
Because one practices with right conduct and is free from deviant karma and other such views regarding the realization of the truths, it is called right action (*samyak-karmānta*).
What is meant by right livelihood (*samyag-ājīva*)?
It is knowing that all forms of livelihood fall into the category of the perverse.

Why is this so? Because those who harbor perceptions of life, perceptions of the existence of all things, and false conceptualizations—yet who maintain the perception of unconditioned nirvana and purity, as well as the perception of seeing the Buddha—and who dwell within this state with a purely focused mind, desiring thereby to sustain a pure livelihood, will all fall into wrong action. All forms of livelihood, if they are true life-sustenance, are not considered wrong; nor does one harbor [attachment to] right livelihood [as a conceptual object]. This is called right livelihood.
To speak of what is wrong livelihood, yet to attain such that all forms of livelihood become entirely pure—this is called right livelihood.

To understand that among all forms of livelihood there is neither right nor wrong, to abide in the practice of pure livelihood without negligence, and to have no livelihood that is right or wrong, neither dual nor singular, neither appropriate nor inappropriate—this is called right livelihood.

One who does not abide in deviance attains pure livelihood; being without the notion of life, without good or speech, and without life or non-life, they practice with true correctness and perceive without falsehood—this is called right livelihood.
"What is called right effort?
It is the relinquishing of all wrong efforts. Why is that?"
All skillful means that fall into perversity are such that wherever the skillful means reside, the mind remains attached; this is called "perverse means. Why is this so?
Because among all dharmas there is no true perverse means;
when the skillful means one practices is not genuine, that lack of genuineness is called "perverse means," for therein is no skillful means at all!

There is no ultimate and no verbal expression; all skillful means are severed, for therein nothing exists. One abandons the notion of *nirvāṇa* and the notion of Buddha-dharma, yet understands the application of all skillful means, knowing that none of them are ultimately real, as they all culminate in the absence of skillful means.

When one acts with equanimity, there is no expedient means; for all dharmas are equal and without distinction. There is no expedient means that transcends directional calculations, and regarding all such directional meanings, there is nothing to be calculated—neither what is appropriate nor what is inappropriate.
This is right expedient means; it is said that such expedient means is ungraspable.

What is called "expedient means" (upāya) refers to the concentrated mind; severing all expedient means refers to the various true truths (satya). To view things with such equanimity is the non-conceptualization of expedient means; because there is nothing to be conceptualized, this is the correct expedient means.
"What is meant by 'right intention'?
All that is thought constitutes wrong perception; all that the mind intends constitutes wrong volition. Why is this so?
All that falls into error—if it arises from the mind, it is entirely erroneous;
for the mind has nothing upon which to dwell.
Why is this? All that is conceived arises from causes and conditions, and what are called causes and conditions are all termed "erroneous."
When the thoughts of one’s mind neither arise nor cease, this is called right mindfulness; for this reason, it is named right mindfulness.

If there is no dwelling place for mental intention and no initiation of karma, and if one is without intention, with the intentionless being the foremost purity, such that all deviant intentions are severed and all discursive thoughts are eliminated—wherein that which is deviant is entirely devoid of mental intention—this is abiding in right intention.

As for its correct intention (*samyak-saṃkalpa*): it is neither improper nor deviant; it is right mindfulness as opposed to wrong mindfulness. Having eliminated all mental intentions and discursive thoughts, that which is clearly understood is a mind that does not give rise to distraction. Constantly practicing these six matters is called "abiding in correct intention."

The mind has never given rise to the notion of "having a mind" nor to the characteristics of a mind; it understands that all minds are fully comprehended as they truly are, and thus one no longer dwells on thoughts of having a mind or not having a mind, of what is appropriate or inappropriate. This is to abide in right mindfulness, free from both mind and error.

To contemplate equanimity through neither mindfulness nor non-mindfulness, being without cause, without thought, and without anything to be conceived; to reach the state of wordlessness where all expectations are absent; to abide in the equality of reflection where there is neither intention nor non-intention; to be without speech or discourse, having cast aside all words; to understand according to the true reality; and to be universally without teaching, without thought, and without conceptualization—this is what is called abiding in equanimity.
"What is called right concentration?
It is to see that all concentrations are, in fact, wrong concentrations. Why is this so?"

If one perceives the conceptualizations that serve as the conditions for samādhi, and yet hopes for or becomes attached to them, these are all false concentrations; such is called "taking the opposite," and this concentration is not true.

If, regarding all sensations, there is nothing experienced, and one does not harbor the seeking of the conceptualization of samādhi-concentration, being without the teachings of transcendence and without the mental state of recollective concentration—being without dependence, without fabrication, and without expansion, having extinguished and severed joy, remaining eternally secluded in peace and bliss, and discerning the characteristics of concentration—such that one dwells in no place within samādhi-concentration, this is what is named "Right Concentration Samādhi."

"What is called right concentration (samyak-samādhi) is that which is without attachment to any state of meditative absorption; it is non-negligence and clarity like wisdom, thoroughly understanding the intent of concentration without relying on the practice of concentration. It is free from longing and equalizes right practice; thus, when there is neither perception, nor non-perception, nor the perception of non-perception, it is called right concentration."
Without right and without wrong, with all expectations gone; having severed all conceptualizations and extinguished all desires, this is called right concentration (*samyaksamādhi*).
That which is called "concentration" is neither right nor wrong concentration; the mind does not arise, being neither unrighteous nor wrong—there is no right concentration and no wrong concentration.

Why is this? Because by being able to awaken to and understand the various meditative concentrations (*samādhi*) through skillful means (*upāya*), one abides in right concentration (*samyak-samādhi*).
Being free from the notion of "concentration" (*samādhi-saṃjñā*), and not accumulating [even] equanimity—which is universally called "all"—is what is termed right concentration.

He does not race about nor indulge in idle diversions; whether in states of equanimity or error, he views all phenomena with universal equanimity. With all his mind concentrated, he abides in right meditative attainment (*samāpatti*). He perceives through wisdom that the entire triple world is conditioned (*saṃskṛta*), and he beholds the true reality (*satya*) regarding the births and transmigrations within all five destinies.
The Buddha said:
"Dhāraṇīdhara!

When a bodhisattva thus understands the meaning of the Way, attains such discernment of the course of the Way, and through these holy practices fully elucidates the True Reality, this is called Right Concentration."
The Scripture of the Bodhisattva Dhṛtipāla, Scroll Three.
The Scripture of the Bodhisattva Dhṛtipāla, Scroll Four.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Zhu Fahu of the Yuezhi during the Western Jin Dynasty.
Chapter Ten: The Mundane and the Transcendent.
The Buddha addressed the Bodhisattva Dhāraṇīdhara:
"What is meant by a bodhisattva attaining clear understanding of the essentials of the scriptures concerning the mundane and the transcendent?"
What is meant by "transcending the present world"?
If there is a bodhisattva who constantly and correctly contemplates transcending the present world,
how does one contemplate correctly?
What are called the dharmas of the present world?
What are called the dharmas that transcend the world?
If there are those who abide in inverted dharmas, their practices all arise from perception; they are produced by causes and conditions and conjoin with the false.
There are two conditions for the establishment [of speech], arising from two types of conceptualization:
first, from falsehood; second, from non-arising.

This false speech is a deceptive and delusive phenomenon that results in ignorant and deluded contemplation, like that of a small child who grasps at various kinds of drawings in the void and falsely wanders about.
Ignorant and deluded ordinary people imagine that there is a world;
they calculate that all worldly things ultimately return to ruin and decay, dispersing and being utterly exhausted.

Because they see that all worldly phenomena arise from falsehood and delusion, and because their causes are unconditioned and fundamentally non-arisen, the aggregates (*skandha*), elements (*dhātu*), and sense bases (*āyatana*) all arise from the conjunction of conditions. Regarding form, sound, smell, taste, and touch, these exist through the law of dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*), yet one does not speak of "form" as a condition in itself.
It is because the minds of foolish ordinary beings have attachments that various views arise from countless perspectives, leading to clinging and fixation.

If that fundamental nature is left neglected and impoverished, it causes worldly views to abide in perversion; when one observes worldly phenomena and supramundane phenomena as being therein, what can be said to be correct?

If worldly phenomena were truly as they appear, then realizing their fundamental purity would constitute transcending the world; yet one clearly understands that the world cannot be sought after and is ultimately unobtainable, and the same is true for transcending the world.

"If one cannot attain the transcendence of the world within this present life, and lacks both the karma for the present life and the karma for transcendence, one proclaims that the transcendence of the world and the present life are fundamentally pure by nature.
What is meant by proclaiming the karma of transcending the world? "
If the world is fundamentally pure up to its transcendence of the world, why is this so?
Because it can never be apprehended; the present world is fundamentally pure and entirely empty, and that world is likewise so.

The world is fundamentally natural, and the world is fundamentally pure and quiescent; because the world is naturally pure and quiescent, one should contemplate that worldly dharmas have no ultimate accomplishment. Thus should one observe.

The mundane world and the supramundane world are both unattainable; because they are unattainable, one does not cling to the mundane world, nor does one conceive of the supramundane world. Since one does not conceive of either the mundane or the supramundane, one does not participate in worldly conventions (*saṃvṛti-satya*).

Why is this so? Because one has awakened to and clearly understood that the world is entirely empty, deceptive, and a delusive dharma; because one is able to perceive that the world is dependent and non-existent; and because one does not form conceptions of the world nor harbor aspirations for the transcendence of the world.
"Why is that? The Buddha said, "Dhāraṇīdhara!"
That which is called "the world" refers to the five aggregates of clinging (*pañca-upādāna-skandha*).

One greedily seeks to unite with all worldly phenomena; yet one clearly knows that these aggregates can never be obtained through seeking, for the five aggregates are spontaneously unobtainable, and the five aggregates are fundamentally pure and likewise unobtainable.

The five aggregates have no coming or going and reach nowhere; their point of convergence cannot be found. This is called transcending the world, for one does not know the destination or abode to which the five aggregates return.
Because the five aggregates, the various elements (*dhātu*), and the sense bases (*āyatana*) are fundamentally pure.

"If a bodhisattva contemplates worldly phenomena and perceives nothing at all, thereby conforming to transcendence; and if they do not perceive transcendence as being conjoined with the world, then there is no world, but only the vision of transcendence."
In transcending the world, one does not perceive worldly dharmas as having any distinct maintenance.
One does not differentiate between two types of dharmas, saying, "This is a worldly dharma; this is a supramundane dharma."
Why is this so? O Dhāraṇīdhara!
In whatever world one may dwell, one understands that the beginning and end of the world are fundamentally non-existent, and the transcendence of the world is likewise so.

Although one perceives the existence of the world, there are in fact no worldly phenomena; the conceptualizations regarding both the mundane and the supramundane are identical, for one has realized that the world does not exist.
Suppose there were someone who thought to themselves:
"The mundane is distinct, and the supramundane is different."

Thus, for such a person, a Buddha does not appear in the world; yet even if a Buddha appears in the world, the entire world is inverted, and they lack the resolve to practice the Way through authentic understanding. Using wisdom to examine the world and proclaiming the Dharma, one dwells amidst the inversions of the world and saves those who greedily cling to it; therefore, this is called "crossing over the world."
Therefore, Dhāraṇīdhara!
By means of correct understanding and examining with wisdom, one clearly comprehends the inversions of the world; thus it is called "transcending the world.

When the Tathāgata appears in the world, he universally encompasses all dharmas; there is no duality between the mundane and the transcendent. Through correct wisdom, he observes, realizes, and attains them, and therefore proclaims the Dharma for transcending the world.
The Buddha said, “Dhāraṇīdhara! One does not wander in the world by means of these dharmas;

there is no place to which one goes, nor anything to be eliminated. By not relying on worldly disputes, one attains the meaning of the world; by not being mindful of transcending the world, one understands worldly terminology. To penetrate fundamental conceptions and yet become attached to dualistic notions—failing to understand how to penetrate such dharmas as these—is to lack deliverance; one cannot comprehend or skillfully traverse the world.”
Why is this? Because they employ two modes of practice, and those who employ these two modes cannot comprehend either the mundane or the supramundane.
When a bodhisattva thus uses skillful means to understand all phenomena, there is nothing—whether pertaining to the present world or the world beyond—that he does not master.
Chapter Eleven: Conditioned and Unconditioned. From the *Dhāraṇīdhara-paripṛcchā-sūtra*, Chapter Eleven: "Conditioned and Unconditioned. The Buddha addressed Dhāraṇīdhara:
"What is meant by a bodhisattva who clearly understands and discerns conditioned and unconditioned phenomena?"
What are conditioned and unconditioned phenomena?
If there is a bodhisattva who, through correct awakening, seeks conditioned and unconditioned phenomena in accordance with principle.
What is meant by "in accordance with principle"?
How is it sought?

One does not create conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*); one who has insight into this naturally attains the title [of "Buddha"]. Because one has already produced conditioned things, they are called "conditioned," and furthermore, conditioned phenomena evolve through falsehood.
