What is meant by "transformation" (*parāvṛtti*)?

It is because things have already converged and naturally return [to their source], that the teaching on the fundamental limit of conditions (*pratyaya-pūrvānta*) is established through two conditions.

All phenomena arise from their own respective causes; there is no creator who acts as an instigator. Having arisen spontaneously, these conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*) are themselves the natural law, for they do not involve a turning back [to a prior agent]; thus they are called "conditioned."

These conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*) have no interior, no exterior, and no middle; they exist as deceptive delusions, neither uniting nor dispersing. They arise from false conceptualization (*vikalpa*), and through the condition of ignorance (*avidyā*), deluded karma gives rise to all phenomena. These proceed spontaneously, performing actions without instruction or deliberate formation. From these conditioned things, one grasps at their characteristics; because of this inversion, foolish worldlings cling to names. Furthermore, the wise person realizes that conditioned phenomena cannot be found at their limits; not clinging to the conditioned and not uniting with existent dharmas—this is called being wise.
"Discerning with wisdom reaches the ultimate reality; whatever conditioned activities are performed, they are all brought to cessation.

Discerning with wisdom analyzes all conditioned phenomena as empty, deceptive, and illusory; these dharmas are entirely non-existent, being both spontaneous and yet devoid of spontaneity, arising from mental intention to constitute all that is conditioned."
Why is this? One should not practice the causal conditions of the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*).
If one understands the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), one will never again practice the conduct of conditioned causes; only when one understands the unconditioned does one attain penetration.
How is this understood? All conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta*) are unreal and formless; they are entirely without limit and have no point of convergence.

When the wise observe them, they do not regard conditioned phenomena as reaching a final state of arising. These conditioned phenomena are without any objective basis and are entirely non-differentiated; furthermore, there is no difference between the arising of the conditioned and the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*). One proclaims the severing of the karma of conditioned phenomena—distinguishing "this is conditioned" from "this is unconditioned," and "this is the characteristic of the conditioned" from "this is the characteristic of the unconditioned."
What is meant by the characteristics of the conditioned?
It is knowing that birth leads to death, and that meeting results in separation.
What is meant by the characteristics of the unconditioned?
Non-arising and non-ceasing are neither meeting nor distinct.

Foolish, ignorant worldlings cannot understand or enter into these two meanings; they do not comprehend the characteristics by which conditioned phenomena arise or the characteristics by which they perish. They do not abide in the characteristic of difference, yet because of the arising of the characteristic of non-existence, they abide in difference.

"If these characteristics did not exist, that which the Tathāgata has spoken would not arise from these characteristics, nor would it cease from these characteristics, nor would it abide in such characteristics.
The Buddha said:
"Dhṛtipāla!"
The Tathāgata has said that all dharmas are without marks; this is because they can be realized as having no mark of arising, no mark of cessation or destruction, and no mark of abiding.

The Tathāgata expounds the characteristic of the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*); this characteristic is no-characteristic. Those who possess conditioned characteristics cannot become guides of the unconditioned. Therefore, the Dharma taught by ignorant and deluded ordinary beings arises from the conditioned and ultimately returns to extinction; only the unconditioned is peace.
Because it is unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), neither arising nor ceasing, and likewise having no place of abiding, it is called "unconditioned.

That which follows from habitual practice gives rise to arising and ceasing; that which has no habitual practice is without exhaustion. It is without activity, without exhaustion, and without any distinct place of abiding.

By means of true and correct understanding, one realizes this wisdom: that there is no conjunction, no arising, and no cessation, nor is there any abiding in difference. "If there is a bodhisattva, they should contemplate in this way:

regarding conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*) and unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta-dharma*), they do not perceive them as either non-existent or as having permanence, but rather as they truly are. They do not perceive conditioned phenomena or unconditioned phenomena; the conditioned does not see the unconditioned, and the unconditioned does not see the conditioned. They do not perceive any distinction from the unconditioned, yet they still think to themselves: 'My body exists!'"
True existence is precisely the perception of conditioned phenomena; there is nothing else that exists as a conditioned reality.

Through contemplation and the cessation of delusive thoughts, one realizes that both conditioned and unconditioned dharmas are eternally devoid of conceptualization. By means of this non-conceptualization, one discerns all perceptions, severs all attachments, and thereby comprehends the unconditioned. Having removed all conditions, one returns to the fundamental purity of being without conditions.
Its cause is fundamentally pure, and what is perceived therein is truly real. Because one can clearly understand that there is nothing at all to be done, there is no conjunction.

When a bodhisattva is able to attain this state of both the conditioned and the unconditioned, they then realize that all phenomena are neither existent nor non-existent, and furthermore do not rely upon the conditioned or the unconditioned; it is only then that they attain perfect enlightenment.
The Buddha told Dhāraṇīdhara:

"If there is a bodhisattva who discriminates the five aggregates (skandhas), thoroughly understands the various elements (dhātus), and comprehends the six sense bases (āyatanas); who is able to fully know the twelve links of dependent origination (pratītyasamutpāda) and analyze the four foundations of mindfulness (smṛtyupasthāna), the five faculties (indriya), and the eightfold path; who can awaken to the activities of both the mundane and the supramundane, and clearly understand the matters of the conditioned (saṃskṛta) and the unconditioned (asaṃskṛta)."

By clearly understanding this, one attains the realization that all dharmas are non-existent; one proclaims that which all dharmas cannot reach, gains mastery over the power and force of meaning, and thoroughly explains the chapters and phrases of all dharmas. One severs the mind of birth, old age, and death—which cannot be destroyed—and is able to personally perfect the unsurpassed, right, and true path, achieving supreme, perfect enlightenment.
Chapter Twelve: The Bodhisattva Ratnaprabha. In the *Dhāraṇīdhara-paripṛcchā-sūtra*, Chapter Twelve, "The Bodhisattva Ratnaprabha," the Buddha addressed Dhāraṇīdhara:
"In the distant past, incalculable, immeasurable, and infinitely vast eons ago."

At that time, there was a Buddha in the world named King of Purple Gold Mountain Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Perfect in Knowledge and Conduct, Sugata, Knower of the World, Unsurpassed One, Tamer of Men, Teacher of Gods and Humans, the Buddha, the World-Honored One.

The lifespan of that Tathāgata King of the Purple Gold Mountain was five kalpas; the assembly of śrāvakas was incalculable, and the gathering of bodhisattvas was likewise limitless, such that no one could fully enumerate or comprehend their number.

That land is flourishing; wind and rain fall in their proper seasons, and the five grains ripen in abundance. The people are peaceful and secure; the strong do not oppress the weak, and each finds their rightful place. Their mental conduct is impartial, their food and drink are digested without causing illness, and their lust, anger, and delusion are thin. They cultivate themselves with virtue, and their households abide in righteous instruction, following the precepts in purity.

At that time, the Tathāgata, for the sake of all bodhisattvas and all sentient beings, resolved their nets of doubt so that none harbored resentment, and proclaimed the treasury of the bodhisattva path and its teachings.

At that time, there was a bodhisattva named Ratnaprabha who, upon hearing the Buddha expound these deeds of the bodhisattvas—namely, the aggregates (*skandhas*), the bases (*āyatanas*), the elements (*dhātus*), the eighteen aspects, the twelve links of dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*), the sense faculties, the foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*), the practice of the eightfold noble path, the mundane and the supramundane, and the conditioned and the unconditioned—immediately accepted and upheld them.

Thus he practiced with such diligence for twelve hundred million years, never giving rise to thoughts of lust, anger, or delusion; he did not crave gain, offerings, food, drink, clothing, bedding, seats, or medicinal treatments for illness; he cultivated his mind with focused refinement, entering into such meditative contemplations of clear understanding, constantly practicing diligence until the end of his life, purely cultivating the holy life (*brahmacarya*).

After his life has ended in the presence of that Buddha, he returns to his native land; as soon as he is born among humans and touches the ground, he again leaves the household life and once more receives this training, thus clearly understanding and practicing such a semblance-dharma (*saddharma-pratirūpaka*).

Furthermore, for sixty billion years in that realm, he purely cultivated the Brahma-faring with a mind that never abandoned or distanced itself from it; thus, his aspiration for such a Dharma was pursued without ceasing, and at the end of his life, he returned to be born in a Buddha-land.

The Tathāgata King of the Purple Gold Mountain remained in existence and continued to cultivate the pure Brahma-conduct in that place; within each eon, he was born and passed away five times, ending and beginning again.

"When that Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha King of the Purple Jewel Mountain was about to enter parinirvāṇa after the completion of five kalpas, [the Bodhisattva]—due to this exemplary model—became widely learned and immeasurable, thoroughly understanding all dharmas that he had heard and received throughout those five kalpas."

Having observed this, he consulted the Buddha for further explanation; attaining the power of that intention, he gazed upon the Tathāgata and then expounded the teaching one by one for the sake of sentient beings, awakening immeasurable people, all of whom gave rise to the aspiration for supreme, perfect, and true enlightenment.

After the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, the True Dharma shall remain in the world for one kalpa; furthermore, he will come and go and circulate there five hundred times, being born among humans and always leaving the household life to study. He will revere this exemplary model and master the orthodox scriptures, transforming countless and inconceivable classes of sentient beings so that they all enter the ultimate practice.
The Bodhisattva Jewel Light saw ten trillion Buddhas; the last among them was a Buddha named Immeasurable Light Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, who bestowed upon him this prediction:

"After incalculable kalpas, you shall attain the unsurpassed, right, and true path. After further incalculable kalpas, you shall again encounter hundreds of thousands of myriads of koṭis of Buddhas, and having attained perfect enlightenment, you shall be known as the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha Resolving All Doubts."
The assembly of śrāvakas was incalculable and beyond measure, and the assembly of bodhisattvas was countless.
In that land, the human lifespan was two kalpas; rice and grain were common and inexpensive, and the people lived in peace and security.
"Therefore, Dhāraṇīdhara!
A bodhisattva mahāsattva who wishes to attain such a model and to clearly understand this correct scripture should diligently study, receive, uphold, recite, and chant the essentials of this sūtra."
The Buddha again addressed Dhṛtarāṣṭra:
"If there is a bodhisattva who studies this sutra, they shall attain skillful means and constantly cultivate four dharmas. What are these four?"

First, to leave home and abandon one's occupation to become a śramaṇa; second, to forsake clamor and bustle to practice dwelling in seclusion; third, to abide in pure precepts and conduct without violation or deficiency; fourth, to distance oneself from indolence and cultivate diligent contemplation without ceasing—these are the four.
By practicing these four, one diligently seeks extensive learning, constantly establishes patience, and swiftly attains the four dharmas.

What are the four? First, although born in the world, one always dwells in a central land; second, by encountering the era of a Buddha, one does not reside in a frontier region; third, one always upholds the True Dharma and never opposes it; fourth, one completely eliminates the veil of transgressions so that no further calamities remain. These are the four.

If there is a bodhisattva who studies such essential sūtras as these, they will immediately attain power and influence: their generosity will be pure, their precepts untainted, and they will possess patience, diligence, single-mindedness, and wisdom; being sagely and luminous without flaw, they establish these dharmas to achieve skillful means.
"Furthermore, Dhāraṇīdhara!

A bodhisattva who studies these established merits of knowing contentment and dwelling in seclusion conceives an immeasurable compassion for sentient beings. By means of this great compassion, they enter among sentient beings, and only thereafter do they study such dharmas as these to understand their essential practice."
"Furthermore, that bodhisattva enters the gateway of dhāraṇī and trains in diligent cultivation.
What is meant by entering the gateway of dhāraṇī and training in diligent cultivation?
It is to aspire with earnest intent, to contemplate with diligence, to clearly understand the measure of phenomena, and through skillful means to observe and uphold boundless practices."

Furthermore, they understand and contemplate the various gateways of meditative concentration and the essential dharma-gates; they enter into immeasurable causal conditions and right practices, attaining such power and majesty as these. They comprehend all dharmas and discern their distinctions, attaining the power and majesty of the mind through such clear understanding. They sever birth, old age, sickness, and death; with firm resolve and without cowardice, they do not lose the true Dharma, thereby accomplishing the aspiration for unsurpassed, perfect, and true enlightenment and attaining supreme, right awakening.
The Buddha again addressed Dhāraṇīdhara:

"If there is a bodhisattva who penetrates the gate of dhāraṇī and is universally able to understand the direction of the terminology of all phenomena, using a single matter to enter into hundreds of thousands of matters, and using the power of the Way to discern all phenomena without failing to reach them."
Furthermore, if a bodhisattva attains the gate of concentrated mind and enters into sounds, they then enter the words of the gate of the unlimited mind.

By attaining entry into this, they comprehend various categories of all dharma-gates; by entering the path-gate of all dharmas, they proclaim all teachings so that there are none who do not receive salvation.

Furthermore, that bodhisattva practices wisdom; by the power of this wisdom, they clearly understand all perceptions. Having diligently resolved upon these perceptions, they attain all dharmas through the power of this wisdom, swiftly achieving unhindered penetration.

Furthermore, if a bodhisattva thoroughly understands the practice of the gates of immeasurable meditative concentrations (*samādhi*), by abiding in this stage, they universally attain all the dharmas of the ten directions.

Moreover, if a bodhisattva thoroughly understands the practice of the gates of immeasurable dhāraṇīs and comprehends the power of the gates of incalculable meditative concentrations, using these gates of meditative concentration to elucidate the source of limitless multitudes of dharmas, they enter universally into all dharmas through this path and stage, such that there is nothing they do not penetrate.

Furthermore, that bodhisattva is exceedingly capable of clearly understanding and observing the activities of the world; he thoroughly discriminates between the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) and the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*). While practicing all dharmas, his mind does not become attached to the conditioned or the unconditioned. By practicing all such dharmas, he swiftly understands all phenomena and attains clear wisdom.

Furthermore, when a bodhisattva practices skillful means, they diligently examine that all dharmas are fundamentally without any activity. Although they perform this contemplation, they do not engage in worldly affairs; they do not cling to worldly dharmas nor rely upon them. Through such a dharma as this, they swiftly attain the clear understanding of all dharmas, discerning all dharmas, exercising the power of the mind to bestow wealth and analyze the chapters and phrases, and fulfilling the mental activities that sever birth, old age, and death.
"Therefore, Dhāraṇīdhara!
This is the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva’s perfection of skillful means regarding the dharma. What are the four? "

"Regarding this Dharma-scripture, one should revere it as the true meaning of the Way, diligently cultivate the True Dharma, attain unimpeded mastery in this sutra, and universally enter the wisdom of the Way.
Chapter 13: The Chapter on the Past The *Dharanidhara-bodhisattva-sutra*, Chapter Thirteen: The Chapter on the Past. The Buddha addressed Dharanidhara:
"In the distant past, incalculable kalpas ago, beyond all measure, long and limitless."

At that time, there was a Buddha named Immeasurable Light Transcendent King Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Perfect in Knowledge and Conduct, Sugata, Knower of the World, Unsurpassed One, Tamer of Men, Teacher of Gods and Humans, Buddha, World-Honored One.
During the time of that Buddha, the assembly of śrāvakas was incalculable, the great congregations were limitless, and the assemblies of bodhisattvas were beyond measure.
When that Buddha was in the world, his lifespan lasted for one kalpa.

Furthermore, that buddha-field is entirely covered and formed of the seven treasures; trees made of the seven treasures grow, surrounding it on all sides, adorning every tree with extraordinary and rare jewels that form a canopy of interlaced nets.

Furthermore, beneath every tree there were lion thrones provided; these thrones were draped with fine, exquisite silk and cotton cloths wrapped around the trees. All the thrones had feet made of lapis lazuli, and the trees were inlaid with red pearls. Naturally fragrant incense formed the leaves, and flowers were always in full bloom, encircling them in a spiral.
Before those trees, there are natural bathing pools filled with water of eight virtues; the sand at the bottom of these waters is composed entirely of crystal, musaragalva, and red pearls.
Furthermore, these bathing pools are fashioned from the Three Jewels, and within them grow blue, red, yellow, and white lotuses that arise spontaneously.

Furthermore, the waters of the various ponds are adorned with railings fashioned from the seven treasures; all these railings and the ground are as level as the palm of a hand. Moreover, that buddha-field is pure and free from defilement.

In that buddha-land, jewel trees flourish profusely, like the great Pārijāta tree in the Trāyastriṃśa heaven. Adorned with magnificent moon-bright pearl trees, they fill the buddha-field by the hundreds of millions. Their radiance completely outshines the brilliance of the sun and moon, causing them no longer to appear.

The various jeweled trees were covered with a lattice of rare treasures, emitting beautiful sounds like those of sorrowful peacocks and flocks of birds, as well as the songs and musical sounds of celestial maidens. Such gentle tones flowed everywhere throughout the Buddha-field; there were no three evil realms, nor was any evil committed. No clamorous or confused speech was directed toward sentient beings, but only the exposition of such dharmas as these—the *Prajñāpāramitā*—from the *Bodhisattvapiṭaka*. It transformed countless multitudes of people and beings so that on a single day they all resolved their minds on the Way. Having originally resolved their minds upon the Great Way, they then fully perfected the dharmas of the factors of enlightenment (*bodhipākṣika-dharma*).
"In this way, Dhāraṇīdhara!

That Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha Immeasurable Light Transcendent King, by means of his skillful expedients, has caused incalculable and infinite numbers of sentient beings over countless years to resolve upon the path to enlightenment. He now dwells below this buddha-field, in that other buddha-field, where he is perfecting the practices of a bodhisattva."
After the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, the True Dharma shall remain for half a kalpa; after that, following the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, the True Dharma will then vanish.
At that time, there will be a bodhisattva named Amitamati who comes from a buddha-field in the lower direction to be born in this land.

That land is ten Buddha-worlds away from here. Having been born there not long ago, at the age of sixteen, he abandoned his secular affairs to become a śramaṇa. In the presence of the Buddha King of Immeasurable Radiance and Transcendence, he inquired about and received the sūtras. As the Dharma was nearing its end, he proclaimed for the sake of the bodhisattvas the aggregates (skandhas), elements (dhātus), and all the bases of cognition (āyatanas), analyzing and explaining their meanings. Hearing such diligent practice as this, he dwells within this Dharma of the *pāramitās* and employs the skillful means of expedient liberation.

By virtue of these roots of merit, that land was further cleared; he beheld billions of Buddhas and universally received this Dharma. In every place where he was born, he always remembered his past lives. Throughout his youth, he remained unmarried and purely cultivated the *brahmacarya*. Leaving home out of faith, he became a śramaṇa. In every place where he was born, he attained mastery over the mind, and the bodies he assumed were always endowed with meritorious achievements.

And in his final existence, he shall attain the unsurpassed, true, and correct path, becoming a Most Perfectly Awakened One, titled the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha Immeasurable Radiance Jewel King.

If there are bodhisattvas who wish to swiftly attain Buddhahood, reach all-knowledge, and fulfill the Buddha-way during the final five turbidities when the Dharma is about to perish, they should diligently resolve their will to receive and proclaim such a teaching as this. Exhausting themselves in joyful devotion and constantly practicing with vigor, those who receive this scripture in the final age of decadence shall possess immeasurable merit and virtue. To recite it, uphold it, and explain it for others brings forth blessings beyond compare.

Chapter Fourteen: Bhadrapāla and the Five Hundred Bodhisattvas *Bhadrapāla and the Five Hundred Bodhisattvas*, Chapter Fourteen At that time, the five hundred bodhisattvas headed by Bhadrapāla, together with the bodhisattva Kātyaputra, rose from their seats, knelt with palms joined, and addressed the Buddha, saying:

“World-Honored One, during the final age at the end of time when the Dharma is about to perish, we shall receive this teaching. We will abide in the future world of the five turbidities, protect the true scriptures, uphold this model, recite and maintain it, and explain it widely for others.”
Furthermore, there were countless bodhisattvas who each rose from their seats, knelt with palms joined, and gazed intently at the face of the Buddha, each giving rise to this supreme vow:

“O World-Honored One, in the final age of the last dharma-ending period, we shall don the armor of the great vow and receive this sublime model, following this profound and wondrous wisdom proclaimed by the Buddha.”

May all the roots of merit accumulated by the bodhisattvas and the treasuries of the factors of enlightenment be fully perfected; wherever they dwell or travel, may they protect and uphold the Dharma. Upon hearing this sūtra and its likeness, may they increase their joy and delight, receiving, upholding, reciting, and proclaiming it to those who have not yet attained understanding, so that they may enter deeply into the Great Way.
At that time, the Buddha smiled, and five-colored light issued from his mouth, illuminating the entire trichiliocosm, while the earth shook in six ways.
The Venerable Ānanda immediately rose from his seat, knelt with palms joined, and stepped forward to address the Buddha, saying:
"For what reason does the Buddha smile?"
"Since they laugh, there must be an underlying meaning; that the ground is now shaken by the universal radiance of light.

"Do you see these multitudes of bodhisattvas standing before me, who in the future final age shall protect the True Dharma, donning the armor of great vows to rescue those in peril and distress?"

The Buddha recalled that in incalculable kalpas past, at the abodes of various Buddhas, he had donned such armor of great vows; he had personally received this sutra-dharma from those Buddhas and upheld its three categories, guiding and instructing countless classes of sentient beings so that they might come into the presence of the Buddhas. Having received the meaning of these three categories and accepted this true Dharma, they now stand before the Buddha. Subsequently, when the Dharma is on the verge of extinction in the final age, he will extensively transform and enlighten those sentient beings who have not yet attained realization, causing them to receive the Buddha’s true Dharma of the three categories.

While the Buddhas of the Bhadrakalpa appear in the world, you shall likewise receive the instruction on the three categories of the True Dharma from these thousand Buddhas; furthermore, in future ages, you shall similarly receive it from all the holy Buddhas.
"Ānanda, these sons of good family possess meritorious fame and virtue that cannot be scrutinized;
no one is able to calculate the extent of the sūtras and dharmas they have practiced."
O sons of noble family!

These individuals provide for and honor those who bring peace and security to sentient beings; yet even if the Tathāgata were to proclaim such things as these, those who have received the Right Path and bring peace and security to sentient beings would all fail to believe them.
Those who do not believe will experience unrest for a long night and fall into the evil realms.
Furthermore, Ānanda, I shall manifest a proof for you:

even such beings as these bring peace and security to sentient beings; yet were all sentient beings in the three thousandfold world-system to fall into hell solely because of their perceptions and mental formations.
Suppose a great multitude were in the midst of hell, and a single person were to come and say to those in hell:
"Do not be afraid; I shall provide for each of you individually what is beneficial, and by means of timely skillful methods, I shall deliver you from the suffering and affliction of this great hell."

Thus, he personally rescued each and every one of them and established them in a place of safety; for the sake of each individual, he endured in the hells for countless thousands of years, never once becoming weary or negligent, until all had been brought to peace.
“Ānanda! Would that person’s great compassion and vast pity for sentient beings not increase?
Would they not deliver them from the great hells and establish them in great peace?”
Ānanda said: "Very much! Very much!"
“O God among Gods!

the Buddha said, “Suppose that person were to manifest such sublime supernatural powers (*ṛddhi*), establishing all classes of sentient beings in the foremost peace of conditioned existence, bringing them eternal and boundless joy, and accomplishing great compassion; that the merit and blessings of their universal protection would be beyond what the mind can conceive and beyond what words can fully express.”
The Buddha told Ānanda: "I now tell you this:

suppose that Bodhisattva, from within the great hells, were to deliver countless beings and establish them in eternal peace; and suppose all those beings he thus compassionately gathered together were as many as those previously brought to security and harmony, whom he had enabled to cross over great perils and reach the peace of conditioned existence—whether by a hundredfold, a thousandfold, a hundred-millionfold, or even a trillionfold—that would not equal the merit of a son of good family who receives this sūtra."
Why is this so? Because if one calculates the peace of conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta*) that has arisen, it possesses a limit and an end;

it does not reach the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), nor does it transcend craving, nor does it lead to extinction (*nirvāṇa*), nor does it attain the karma of supernatural powers and perfect enlightenment, nor does it accomplish the essential goal of tranquil resolve and *nirvāṇa*.
"Furthermore, Ānanda!
These bodhisattvas establish for sentient beings the unsurpassed great peace and the karma of omniscience (*sarvajñatā*).

Moreover, these bodhisattvas, through the dharma of a Great Being, resolve to study the Vehicle of the Way; they establish the Buddha-way to deliver all sentient beings, and they establish the stages of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, exhorting and assisting them in the Buddha-dharma to cultivate the bodhisattva practice and abide in the Great Way."

These sons of noble family encourage and assist sentient beings in practicing the Dharma of the Bodhisattvas; they do not merely contemplate the Buddha’s teachings but inquire of the Great Hero, receiving and establishing vast compassion to achieve all-encompassing wisdom—thus their merit is limitless.
The Buddha said,
“Ānanda! By means of this True Dharma, whether in a thousand kalpas or incalculable kalpas— measurable in hundreds of billions of years and kalpas, as vast and remote as this.”

The Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, are never idle; they instruct one another in succession, and for countless billions of hundreds of thousands of koṭis of kalpas, they continue to deliver one another to Buddhahood, their merit being inexhaustible and thus boundless.

Why is this? Because in past ages, hundreds of thousands of millions of Buddhas, having originally dwelt there, practiced the bodhisattva deeds and established the Buddha-way; such beings as these, in every place where they were born, received this sutra and used it to provide mutual encouragement and assistance, thereby attaining the unsurpassed, right, and true path and achieving supreme, perfect enlightenment.

In future ages, countless bodhisattvas will transform and guide immeasurable multitudes; through this encouragement and assistance, they shall fulfill the Buddha-dharma and attain the unsurpassed, true, and correct path.
“In this way, Ānanda!
Those sons of good family who train and establish sentient beings in omniscience and the peace of the unsurpassed Great Way—
those who wish to have the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas as their parents for the sake of the Dharma— are precisely what should be called the parents of the Buddhas’ and Bodhisattvas’ path and Dharma.”

Now these bodhisattvas protect those who take refuge in them so that they may all attain self-reliance; these are the ones known as Aniruddha, Kātyāyana, and the others, numbering five hundred, who are the spiritual parents, and these bodhisattvas protect this true scripture.

Noble sons and noble daughters who do not contravene the Buddha’s teachings, nor sever the root of all-knowledge, shall establish great protection for all sentient beings in the future age when the Dharma is about to perish. Abiding in great compassion, they shall open the way to benefit all; through such encouragement and assistance in the final age, they shall protect them so that they do not fall into evil realms, causing countless billions of bodhisattvas and countless Buddhas alike to praise them!
The meritorious virtues of these sons of noble family cannot be fully exhausted.
Why is this? Because the names and meritorious virtues of these sons of noble family are inconceivable.
The Buddha told Ānanda:
"Over countless kalpas—billions, trillions, and quadrillions—the Buddha has gathered and accumulated this treasure of the True Dharma.
Those sons of noble family who receive this Dharma are as numerous as the countless, incalculable assemblies throughout the ten directions."

"The Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, who travel through infinite lands and currently exist therein, shall all together protect and uphold those who study this Dharma, causing them all to dwell in peace and security.
The Buddha said, "Ānanda!"

In the heavens and throughout the world, all these sons of noble family receive prostrations, reverent salutations, and the seeking of refuge from others; they are praised by all the Buddhas of the ten directions, who manifest the Dharma they expound to those who have not yet attained it.

“Ānanda! The Buddha has already sealed these clansmen with a seal that resolves all doubts. If, in a future age at the end of time, they receive such supreme and correct Dharma as this, upholding, reciting, explaining, and proclaiming it to their fellow students, those sons and daughters of good family will thereby swiftly draw near to the karma of omniscience.”

When the Dharma is on the verge of extinction, those who hear this profound and wondrous scriptural teaching and conceive joy and faith shall be granted a prediction of enlightenment by the Buddha as they practice the Bodhisattva vehicle.
Thus, in the final age, these truly realized ones will protect this Dharma, establishing themselves in it and delighting in the Dharma.
Through the Buddha’s encouragement and assistance, these sons and daughters of noble family do not slander this profound and wondrous Dharma.

The Buddha has already granted them the prediction of enlightenment as followers of the Śrāvaka vehicle; having seen Maitreya Buddha appear in the world, their outflows are exhausted and they are free from craving. Because they have received and upheld this profound and wondrous Dharma, they have never slandered it, thereby attaining this meritorious retribution.
The Buddha said:
"If a bodhisattva studies and hears this profound Dharma and, with faith, joy, and delight, likewise receives a prediction of enlightenment,
they shall, during the time of the Tathāgata Maitreya, leave the household life to study tranquility and further make vows that are truly extraordinary."

The Buddha said, "Noble sons and daughters, you whose roots of virtue are harmonious and supple, and whose meritorious achievements are boundless, have received this profound Dharma and practiced it with diligence at the final end of time when the Dharma is about to perish; your merit is immeasurable and your majesty is thus sublime."
Chapter Fifteen: Entrustment The *Dharanidhara-bodhisattva-sūtra*, Chapter Fifteen: Entrustment. At that time, the Bodhisattva Dharanidhara came forward and addressed the Buddha, saying:

"I pray that the Buddha will establish me as a turner of the Wheel of Dharma, seeking neither fame nor profit. In the final age of the end times, may those who hear this authentic scripture experience joy and manifest delight in receiving its subtle and wondrous meaning. For this reason, may they swiftly understand all dharmas, attain the wisdom of discernment, and quickly master the power of intent; may they analyze and judge all dharmas, clearly comprehend the wisdom of the Path, and maintain mindfulness and non-forgetfulness in whatever place they are born, illuminating the ten directions with the light of the Great Dharma."
The Buddha said,
“Dhāraṇīdhara!
If there is a bodhisattva who contemplates this chapter on dharmas, their karma of great wisdom will be a source of infinite light, and they shall accumulate immeasurable great merit.”

If, in future ages, one receives this Dharma-section, upholds, recites, and reads it, as well as other profound sutras that constitute the Bodhisattva’s treasury, and diligently practices the various pāramitās with a devoted mind, then the causes and conditions of Māra’s deeds will find no opportunity, and one shall not be obscured by the veil of transgressions.

The Buddha has already granted him a prophecy; having seen two or three Buddhas, he shall immediately attain the *anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*. Having attained this forbearance, he shall also attain these unsurpassed factors of enlightenment (*bodhipakṣa-dharma*), personally understanding all phenomena and attaining mastery. He shall adorn and purify a Buddha-field, be fully endowed with *śrāvakas*, receive their teachings, and uphold the practice of a bodhisattva.
"In this way, Dhāraṇīdhara!

The Buddha has issued this seal to sever all doubts; in the final age, one who manifests the karma of mastery over the four meanings, practices the dharma of the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva, receives and protects this sutra, and dons the armor of the great vow."
What are these four?
First, one should recognize that the roots of one's own merit are exceedingly great and infinite, immeasurable and beyond calculation;
second, one should manifest the source of goodness for the sake of all sentient beings.
The third is to consult and receive the essential sūtras of the Tathāgata’s True Dharma;
the fourth is to uphold the treasury of the Dharma—the teachings and transformations proclaimed by countless Buddhas.
These are the four.
"Furthermore, there are four dharmas for protecting the profound Dharma during the final age of the end times.
What are these four?
First, to embrace diligence and receive and practice the True Dharma in an evil and degenerate world."

The second is that if one encounters the most grievous suffering and turmoil of strife against the True Dharma, when those who uphold the Dharma are contending with one another, they transform them to bring about harmony and protect the True Dharma;
the third is that they practice patience and are fully endowed with benevolence and harmony;
the fourth is that even in the final age, their minds harbor no resentment, and as they come and go and move about, they constantly practice compassion.
"These are the four [factors] by which one attains the profound Dharma and swiftly reaches all-knowledge.

At that time, Bhadrapāla, Kātyāyana, the five hundred bodhisattvas, and the other bodhisattvas, having heard the Buddha preach this True Dharma of the Path-factors (mārgāṅga), all stood before the Buddha and thought to themselves:
"In the future final age, we shall protect the True Dharma."
The Buddha rubbed the various bodhisattvas with his right palm and addressed them, saying:
"O sons of noble family!

For countless kalpas, the Buddha has cultivated this unsurpassed, true, and correct path, thereby forming a great treasury of jewels. He underwent immense hardship and endured many calamities to rescue infinite beings and bring them to great peace. He renounced his own bodily security to concern himself for all, and thus attained the Dharma and realized supreme perfect enlightenment to entrust it to you, my benevolent ones."
If there are those who study and recite this Dharma, they shall extensively expound its meaning for the fourfold assembly.
When the three categories of Dharma are about to be destroyed, they should establish and protect them; only then shall they radiate the infinite great light.
The Buddha repeated:
"O sons of noble family!
The Tathāgata is like a father, and you, worthy ones, are like his children."
The Buddha is like a sovereign, and all you virtuous ones are like his ministers.

When the father is compassionate and the son filial, when the ruler is upright and the minister loyal, the world is at peace. For countless kalpas, I have practiced this treasury of the Dharma, morality, and virtue, so that it may be spread far and wide throughout the eight directions, above and below.
“May all devas and humans, through universal compassion and filial piety, take refuge in the Buddha; may the Buddha, with great compassion, deliver them all.
